metadata.title: The comparison of PISA 2015-2018 mathematics trend items based on item response times
metadata.venue: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 computer-based assessment public-use data for Türkiye, restricted to 69 mathematics trend items that were administered across both cycles (matrix sampling implies not every student received every item). The authors report using item-level response times and item characteristics, and they compare cycle differences using t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and Spearman correlations; however, the manuscript does not describe applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is based on descriptive and nonparametric comparisons rather than PV-based achievement estimation, the paper does not document any weight variable usage. As a result, weighting and clustering at school/country levels are not explicitly addressed in the reported methodology.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are item-level response times and derived effort indices (RTE/RTF) based on response-time thresholds, not cognitive achievement scores generated as PISA plausible values. While the authors recode certain response categories as missing (e.g., categories 5, 6, 7, 8) and set invalid/no-response to 0, they do not report a formal missing-data handling strategy for the analytic sample (e.g., whether cases with missing response times were excluded listwise or how missingness was treated in correlations and tests). This is therefore a reporting gap specific to missing response-time/score data in the item-level computations.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Türkiye PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 computer-based assessment public-use data restricted to 69 mathematics trend items common across both cycles. Because only 24 test forms contained the 69 trend items and not all students received the mathematics trend items, the analytic sample was further restricted to students who received these trend items: 2408 students in PISA 2015 and 3718 students in PISA 2018. Response categories 5, 6, 7, and 8 were recoded as missing values, and category 9 (no response) was recoded as 0 using PISA methodology coding rules.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Cycle difference: t-test t=3.49, p<.05; Descriptives: mean MRT 99.38 (2015) vs 118.26 (2018); Item-format Wilcoxon signed-rank tests: all item formats statistically significant (Z reported per format, p=0.00 in Table 2).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 & 2018 (Türkiye) mathematics trend item the study leveraged PISA cycle, item format, mathematical process subscale, and item difficulty to analyze mean item response times, finding that students’ mean response times increased from 99.38 seconds (2015) to 118.26 seconds (2018) with a statistically significant t-test (t=3.49, p<.05). This indicates that the 2018 administration elicited more time-on-task/effortful responding for these trend items, suggesting that cycle-to-cycle comparisons of performance should consider effort-related response-time shifts when interpreting changes in achievement.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2 MRT (sec) and Wilcoxon Z/p: Simple MC computer-scored N=16, 82.20 (2015) vs 98.48 (2018), Z=-3.516, p=0.00; Complex MC computer-scored N=13, 89.52 vs 103.75, Z=-3.296, p=0.00; Open response computer-scored N=22, 98.27 vs 113.84, Z=-4.107, p=0.00; Open response human-coded N=18, 123.13 vs 151.73, Z=-3.724, p=0.00.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 & 2018 (Türkiye) mathematics trend item the study leveraged item format and PISA cycle to analyze response times by format, finding that open-ended items (especially human-coded open responses) produced the longest response times and that response times were higher in 2018 for every item format (all Wilcoxon signed-rank tests significant, p=0.00). This indicates that item-format design choices strongly shape observed time-on-task, implying that effort/engagement interpretations should be format-aware when comparing response-time patterns across cycles.

main_findings.target_variable: Response time by mathematical process subscale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 MRT (sec) and Wilcoxon Z/p: Formulating situations mathematically N=21, 95.62 (2015) vs 116.88 (2018), Z=-4.107, p=0.00; Interpreting/applying/evaluating outcomes N=19, 98.15 vs 115.15, Z=-3.823, p=0.00; Employing concepts/facts/procedures N=29, 102.91 vs 121.30, Z=-4.703, p=0.00.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 & 2018 (Türkiye) mathematics trend item the study leveraged mathematical process subscale and PISA cycle to analyze response times, finding that response times increased in 2018 across all three process categories and that the 'employing mathematical concepts, facts and procedures' process had the highest mean response time in both cycles (102.91 in 2015; 121.30 in 2018). This indicates that cognitive-process demands are reflected in time-on-task, suggesting that effort-sensitive interpretations of PISA trends should be disaggregated by mathematical process rather than treated as uniform across the mathematics domain.

main_findings.target_variable: Correlation between item response time and item parameters
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 4 Spearman correlations between mean item response time and item parameters: 2015 difficulty r=0.26 (p<0.01), discrimination r=0.20 (not significant); 2018 difficulty r=0.27 (p<0.01), discrimination r=0.21 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 & 2018 (Türkiye) mathematics trend item the study leveraged item difficulty, item discrimination, and PISA cycle to examine how item parameters relate to response times, finding a statistically significant positive (moderate) correlation between mean item response time and item difficulty in both cycles (r=0.26 in 2015; r=0.27 in 2018, p<0.01) but no significant correlation with item discrimination. This indicates that harder items tend to consume more time, implying that response-time-based effort indicators may be most informative when interpreted alongside item difficulty, while discrimination may be less useful for explaining time variation.

main_findings.target_variable: Response Time Fidelity (RTF) and rapid-guessing proportion
main_findings.performance_metrics: NT10 method: mean RTF 0.97 (2015) vs 0.98 (2018); rapid-guessing proportion 3% (2015) vs 2% (2018). NT20 method: mean RTF 0.94 (2015) vs 0.96 (2018); rapid-guessing proportion 6% (2015) vs 4% (2018).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 & 2018 (Türkiye) mathematics trend item the study leveraged PISA cycle and item characteristics (including item format patterns discussed in the text) to compute Response Time Fidelity (RTF) using NT10 and NT20 thresholds, finding that mean RTF increased from 0.97 to 0.98 (NT10) and from 0.94 to 0.96 (NT20) while the proportion of rapid-guessing students decreased in 2018. This indicates that students showed relatively more solution-oriented behavior in 2018, suggesting that effort/engagement monitoring in PISA should incorporate response-time fidelity indices to contextualize changes in item-level responding across cycles.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes Türkiye’s PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 computer-based mathematics trend items (69 common items) using item-level response times and response-time effort indices (RTE/RTF). Across the 69 items, mean response time increased from 99.38 seconds (2015) to 118.26 seconds (2018), with a statistically significant t-test (t=3.49, p<.05). Item format strongly shaped response times: open-ended items—especially human-coded open responses—had the highest mean response times, and all item-format comparisons across cycles were significant using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (p=0.00 in Table 2). Response time correlated positively with item difficulty in both cycles (Spearman r=0.26 and r=0.27, p<0.01) but not with item discrimination. Using NT10/NT20 thresholds, mean RTF rose (0.97→0.98; 0.94→0.96) and rapid-guessing proportions declined (3%→2%; 6%→4%). Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight handling and missing-data strategy for item-level recoding, and the fact that the analysis is descriptive/nonparametric rather than PV-based achievement modeling.
